Standard operating procedure · Irvine Division

Irvine Project Lifecycle

Remediation through rebuild — assignment to invoicing.

One Project Manager carries each job the whole way. This procedure describes the seven control points every Irvine Co. project passes through and what each role does at each one. There is no handoff at clearance. What moves between phases is information, not ownership.

Process owner: Division Manager – Irvine  ·  Compliance owner: Project Coordinator Manager

The process

1

Intake & Assignment

New work is logged, authorized, assigned to a Project Manager and region, and visible on the master tracking spreadsheet.

Project Coordinator · Division Manager

2

Scope & Plan

The job is inspected, scoped, estimated, staffed, and placed on a dated work calendar.

Irvine Estimator · Project Manager

3

Execution — Remediation

Field labor, equipment, materials, documentation, safety, and daily client updates are controlled.

Lead Technician — Onsite · Lead Technician — Reporting · Project Manager

4

Quality Control & Clearance

Remediation is inspected, corrected, and cleared before the project moves toward rebuild. Irvine Co. inspects every job, so CELCO inspects every job first.

Irvine Estimator · Project Manager

5

Turnover to Rebuild

Approved scope, budget, photos, clearance, and requirements move into rebuild without stalling. What transfers is information. The Project Manager stays accountable.

Project Manager · Rebuild Superintendent

6

Rebuild

Vendors and crews are scheduled, progress is monitored, quality is inspected as the work goes up, and the client is updated daily.

Rebuild Superintendent · Project Manager

7

Closeout & Billing

Final documentation is complete, deficiencies are corrected, and the file is billing-ready.

Project Manager · Project Coordinator

This document says HOW the work runs. What each role owns lives in that role’s definition. Roles are named by title, never by person, so the procedure stays correct when someone changes seats.

Step by step

1

Intake & Assignment

New work is logged, authorized, assigned to a Project Manager and region, and visible on the master tracking spreadsheet.
Project Coordinator

For the coordinator receiving new Irvine Co. work. Log it, get it authorized, and hand the Project Manager a job that is ready to run.

Done when — The job is set up in DASH, authorization is in place, it appears on the master tracking spreadsheet, and a Project Manager and region are assigned.
Receiving the request
  1. Capture the property, unit or area, full address, onsite contact, and access details.
  2. Record who is authorizing the work and on whose behalf, plus the billing party and any work order or reference number.
  3. Record what happened, when it was discovered, and whether the source is active, stopped, or repaired.
  4. Identify the affected areas and any hazard reported.
  5. Determine the region so the job routes to the correct Project Manager.
Job setup
  • Job created in DASH with the complete header.
  • CompanyCam project created.
  • Row added to the master tracking spreadsheet with stage and owner.
  • Authorization sent for signature.
  • Job file opened and the intake record filed.
Authorization
  • Send the Work Authorization for emergency work. Send the contract for scheduled work.
  • Confirm approval is in place before work begins. This is the coordinator's hold to place.
  • Where a permit may be required, expect the estimator to flag it. Open the permit file as soon as they do.
  • File the executed paperwork the day it comes back.
Handoff to the Project Manager
  • Notify the assigned PM with the intake record, authorization status, and access details.
  • Confirm the PM has acknowledged the assignment — do not assume the notification was seen.
  • Keep the caller updated until the PM or the responding technician takes over communication.
Division Manager

For the Division Manager at the start of each day. Confirm every new job has an owner and nothing is sitting unassigned.

Done when — Every new job has a Project Manager, a region, and a current stage on the master tracking spreadsheet.
Daily review
  1. Review the master tracking spreadsheet and the status of every active remediation and rebuild project.
  2. Confirm every new job is assigned to the correct Project Manager and region.
  3. Review jobs pending scheduling, scheduled but not started, in progress, pending clearance, awaiting rebuild, delayed, or requiring escalation.
  4. Confirm field schedules, staffing assignments, and resource coverage for the day.
Assignment rules
  • Jobs route by region to the Project Manager who owns it.
  • Rebalance across regions when service or schedule is at risk — say so explicitly rather than letting a queue build.
  • A job is not assigned until it has a named Project Manager, regardless of which region it fell in.
Escalate the same day when
  • A job has no owner, no authorization, or no access.
  • Staffing or equipment will not cover the day's commitments.
  • A client concern arrives above the Project Manager.
  • Anything affects the division's standing with the client.
2

Scope & Plan

The job is inspected, scoped, estimated, staffed, and placed on a dated work calendar.
Irvine Estimator

For the estimator scoping new remediation work. Estimate what the job actually requires, and flag what will slow it down later.

Done when — The estimate reflects the work required, permit needs are identified and communicated, and the approved scope is in the hands of the Project Manager and Project Coordinator.
Inspection
  1. Travel to the community and inspect the loss.
  2. Photo-document the inspection in CompanyCam and notate the job file in DASH.
  3. Identify affected materials and areas, including adjacent, above, below, and concealed areas.
  4. Confirm the conditions against what was reported at intake.
Writing the estimate
  • Estimate to Irvine Co.'s guidelines and standards, applying Irvine-specific pricing within Division budget ceilings.
  • Estimate the work actually required to complete the project properly — not only what is easy to defend.
  • Identify the rooms and areas the approved scope covers. The technicians work to that boundary.
Permits
  • Determine whether the project will require a city permit.
  • Notify the Project Coordinator as soon as a permit is required so the process can start.
  • Build permit lead time into the scope and any schedule you issue.
Handoff
  • Hand the approved scope to both the Project Manager and the Project Coordinator.
  • Stay reachable for clarification while the PM plans the work — a question answered now is cheaper than a revision later.
Project Manager

For the Project Manager receiving an approved scope. Plan the work, build the crew, and put the job on a dated calendar.

Done when — The job is staffed, scheduled on a dated calendar, entered on your regional view of the tracking spreadsheet, and the client knows when work begins.
Reviewing the scope
  1. Read the approved Scope of Work and the estimate before scheduling anything.
  2. Confirm the rooms and areas included, and what is to be removed.
  3. Raise any gap with the estimator now rather than discovering it onsite.
  4. Confirm authorization is in place with the Project Coordinator.
Staffing and scheduling
  • Assign the technicians the job requires and build the crew around it.
  • Name the Lead Technician for the job — they report to you for its duration.
  • Place the job on a dated work calendar.
  • Publish your schedule daily so the division knows where you will be.
Cost control from day one
  • Know the budget before the first day of work, not at invoicing.
  • Track labor, materials, equipment, and subcontractor cost against it as the job runs.
Client kickoff
  • Tell the client when work begins, what will happen, and who will be onsite.
  • Set the daily update expectation up front. The client receives an update every day the job is active.
3

Execution — Remediation

Field labor, equipment, materials, documentation, safety, and daily client updates are controlled.
Lead Technician — Onsite

For the Lead Technician running the job onsite. Work the approved scope, and know exactly where your authority to expand it ends.

Done when — The approved scope is worked correctly to procedure and additional findings are documented. The PM has approved any work beyond the approved areas. The jobsite is left clean and properly set up.
Before you start
  1. Read and understand the approved Scope of Work — what is to be removed, which areas are included, and what the recommendations require.
  2. Confirm access, the onsite contact, and any restriction on the unit or common areas.
  3. Raise anything unclear with your Project Manager before work begins.
Onsite procedure
  • Follow proper remediation procedure on every project — floor protection, containment, demolition, cleanliness, and equipment setup.
  • Set up, operate, and monitor drying equipment. Track readings to completion.
  • Direct the Assistant Technician's work on the job.
  • Leave the jobsite clean and properly set up before leaving each day.
Additional findings and scope creep
  • Work the conditions onsite, not only the paper — look for affected materials the scope did not anticipate.
  • INSIDE the approved rooms and areas: update the floor plan to document the additional work, and proceed.
  • BEYOND the approved rooms and areas: stop. Obtain Project Manager approval before performing any additional work.
  • When scope extends, update the floor plan to identify the additional affected areas, explain the work required, and supply supporting photos. Never assume additional work is approved. When in doubt, ask the PM.
Lead Technician — Reporting

For the same Lead Technician, before leaving the jobsite. The office cannot schedule the next phase from what is in your head.

Done when — The day's work is photographed and reported by email before you leave the jobsite, including the current timeline, and any milestone reached has been passed on.
Photo documentation
  • Clear before, during, and after photos.
  • Affected materials and additional findings.
  • Containments and equipment setup.
  • Work performed and final conditions.
  • All required photos taken before leaving the site.
Reporting before you leave
  • Send your job update by EMAIL before leaving the jobsite each day — job updates no longer go through Slack.
  • State the current status, work completed, equipment left onsite, additional findings, and next steps.
  • Include the timeline in every update, reflecting current progress and any change to the anticipated completion date.
  • Report concerns or changes to your Project Manager immediately — do not save them for the daily update.
  • SLACK EXCEPTION — demolition complete: notify the Irvine Estimator, so the rebuild estimate can be written the next day.
  • SLACK EXCEPTION — final cleaning complete: notify your Project Manager, so they can perform their quality inspection.
  • These two are scheduling triggers. Never save a milestone for the end of the job. The next phase cannot be booked without it.
Project Manager

For the Project Manager while remediation is running. Keep the job visible, the crew supported, the cost controlled, and the client informed.

Done when — Every active job in your regions is updated daily, the client has had an update, and every decision waiting on you has been made.
Daily control
  1. Read the Lead Technician's update on every active job.
  2. Update your regional view of the tracking spreadsheet — including jobs in the drying phase.
  3. Visit your jobs. Projects are not managed from the office.
  4. Clear anything blocking the field before the end of the day.
Managing the crew
  • Lead Technicians report to you on job status, concerns, additional findings, delays, and questions.
  • Answer scope questions the same day — a technician waiting on you is a crew standing still.
  • Approve or decline additional work beyond the approved rooms and areas. This decision is yours alone.
  • Hold the crew to procedure, documentation, and site standards.
Cost control
  • Track cost against budget as the job runs.
  • Where scope has changed, tell the estimator what must be added or revised so a change order can be submitted.
  • Respond promptly when a revision is requested — invoicing waits on it.
Client communication
  • Send the client a daily update on every active project — including days when no onsite work is performed.
  • Carry the timeline into every update.
  • You own client communication for this job through every phase. It does not pass to anyone else.
4

Quality Control & Clearance

Remediation is inspected, corrected, and cleared before the project moves toward rebuild. Irvine Co. inspects every job, so CELCO inspects every job first.
Irvine Estimator

For the estimator onsite writing the rebuild estimate. You are the first set of eyes on finished remediation — use them.

Done when — A preliminary quality check is complete and anything incomplete has been raised to the Project Manager before the project moves toward rebuild.
Preliminary quality check
  1. While onsite to write the rebuild estimate, walk the completed remediation work.
  2. Confirm the approved Scope of Work was performed.
  3. Identify incomplete work, quality concerns, and anything needing attention.
  4. Raise all of it to the assigned Project Manager the same day.
What this check is, and is not
  • It surfaces problems early, while a technician can still be sent back cheaply.
  • It does NOT clear the job. The Project Manager owns the final inspection and the clearance decision.
  • Report what you found — do not direct the correction yourself.
While you are there
  • Write the rebuild estimate.
  • Prepare a TENTATIVE rebuild schedule to issue with it.
  • Confirm whether the rebuild will require a permit, and notify the Project Coordinator if so.
Project Manager

For the Project Manager closing out remediation. Yours is the inspection that clears the job.

Done when — You have personally inspected the project, confirmed the complete approved scope was performed, and sent the post-evaluation request.
Final remediation inspection
  1. Wait for the technician to confirm the job is dry and final cleaning is complete.
  2. Go to the site and inspect it yourself.
  3. Confirm the complete approved Scope of Work was performed properly.
  4. Send the technician back for anything incomplete, and re-inspect before proceeding.
Every job, not a sample
  • Irvine Co. requires an inspection on every job. The division cannot rely on sampling.
  • Training & Technical Quality audits to the company standard across all divisions. That is a separate check and does not replace yours.
  • Act on anything the estimator raised during their preliminary check.
Clearance
  • Once the project is ready, send the post-evaluation request in your update.
  • Record the clearance on the tracking spreadsheet.
  • Tell the client where the project stands and what happens next.
5

Turnover to Rebuild

Approved scope, budget, photos, clearance, and requirements move into rebuild without stalling. What transfers is information. The Project Manager stays accountable.
Project Manager

For the Project Manager moving a cleared job into rebuild. You are not handing the project over. You are bringing the field team in.

Done when — The rebuild calendar is finalized with real dates, the vendor or in-house crew is assigned, and the client has the start date, quality-inspection date, and calendar.
Finalizing the calendar
  1. Take the estimator's tentative schedule as the starting point.
  2. Finalize it with actual phases and dates once clearance is achieved and work is ready to begin.
  3. Confirm every date before it goes out.
  4. Send the client the start date, the quality-inspection date, and the rebuild calendar.
Bringing in the field team
  • Work with the Rebuild Superintendent to assign a rebuild vendor or in-house technicians.
  • Give them the approved scope, the budget, the photos, and the clearance record.
  • Confirm the Superintendent has what they need before the first day.
  • Confirm permit status with the Project Coordinator — a permit outstanding is a start date that will move.
Update the distribution
  • Update the email thread as the project moves into rebuild: add ICAC-STR@celcoservices.com and remove ICAC-TEAM@celcoservices.com.
  • The thread follows the phase. The ownership does not.
What does not change
  • You remain accountable for scope, cost, schedule, and outcome.
  • You continue to send the client's daily updates.
  • There is no formal handoff and no turnover package. You never left the project.
Rebuild Superintendent

For the Superintendent picking up a cleared job. Get ahead of the materials and the vendors before day one.

Done when — The vendor or crew is briefed, materials are staged or ordered, and the first week of the calendar is achievable.
Before the first day
  1. Read the approved rebuild scope and the finalized calendar.
  2. Confirm the assigned vendor or in-house crew understands the scope and the dates.
  3. Identify the materials the first phase requires.
  4. Raise anything in the calendar you do not believe is achievable — before it starts, not after it slips.
Materials
  • Check what the staging hub already holds.
  • Tell the company warehouse team what is needed and when — purchasing and vendor ordering stay with them.
  • Coordinate transfers from the main warehouse and deliveries to the jobsite.
  • Material gaps are avoidable delays. Get ahead of them.
Permits and inspections
  • Handle permits that require in-person filing or field coordination with the municipality.
  • Schedule the required city inspections and attend where the jurisdiction requires it.
  • Keep the Project Coordinator current so permit status stays tracked in the job file.
6

Rebuild

Vendors and crews are scheduled, progress is monitored, quality is inspected as the work goes up, and the client is updated daily.
Rebuild Superintendent

For the Superintendent running rebuild in the field. Catch problems while they are still cheap, and keep the Project Manager able to speak to the client.

Done when — The assigned Project Manager has an accurate daily picture of every active rebuild, and no defect has been left for the client to find.
Daily field operations
  1. Oversee day-to-day field operations on every active rebuild.
  2. Support subcontractors and in-house technicians with whatever keeps the work moving.
  3. Address field concerns, delays, and material needs before they reach the schedule.
  4. Confirm progress against the approved calendar.
Quality control in progress
  • Inspect rebuild work as it goes up — not only when it is finished.
  • Confirm the work follows the approved Scope of Work and meets CELCO's quality standard.
  • Communicate incomplete work and defects to the vendor or technician AND to the assigned Project Manager.
  • Re-inspect corrections. A defect reported is not a defect fixed.
Reporting to the Project Manager
  • Give the assigned PM a daily update on progress and status.
  • Report delays, concerns, and timeline changes the moment they are identified. The PM's client update is only as accurate as your report.
  • Raise concerns as they arise, never at project completion.
  • Client communication runs through the PM. Field information flows to the PM, who carries it to the client.
Photo documentation
  • Progress of the work as it advances.
  • Work completed at each phase.
  • Any concern identified, before correction.
  • Final completion.
  • Photos show the state of the work, not merely that someone was onsite.
Final rebuild inspection
  • Perform the final inspection once rebuild work is complete.
  • Correct everything found before the client's inspection. The goal is no failed inspections and no return trips.
  • Tell the Project Manager the project is ready, and what you corrected to get it there.
Project Manager

For the Project Manager during rebuild. The Superintendent runs the field. The outcome is still yours.

Done when — The client has had a daily update with a current timeline, the budget is intact, and the project is ready for the client's inspection.
Daily control
  1. Read the Superintendent's daily field report.
  2. Send the client a daily update with the current timeline.
  3. Update the tracking spreadsheet.
  4. Clear decisions the field is waiting on.
Cost and change orders
  • Track rebuild cost against the approved budget.
  • When a rebuild revision is needed, confirm it and state what must be added or changed so the estimator can submit the change order.
  • Respond promptly — invoicing waits on it.
Subcontractor invoices
  • Review subcontractor invoices as they arrive for approval.
  • Approve or reject promptly. A held invoice becomes a vendor who will not schedule you.
  • Where an invoice cannot be approved, determine whether the numbers do not match or the estimate needs revising, and say which.
Accountability at the final inspection
  • The Superintendent performs the rebuild inspections.
  • You remain accountable for whether the project passes the client's inspection.
  • If it fails, that is a project outcome, not a field outcome.
7

Closeout & Billing

Final documentation is complete, deficiencies are corrected, and the file is billing-ready.
Project Manager

For the Project Manager closing the project. Confirm the money before the file leaves your hands.

Done when — The job is within budget, every revision is captured, documentation is complete, and the file has been released for invoicing.
Before releasing for invoicing
  • Complete approved scope performed and inspected.
  • All deficiencies corrected and re-inspected.
  • Every change order and revision submitted and reflected.
  • Subcontractor invoices reviewed and approved or rejected.
  • Job confirmed within budget.
  • Photo documentation complete from first response to final completion.
Budget confirmation
  • Confirm the job is within budget before it goes to invoicing. This is the last point at which a discrepancy is cheap to fix.
  • Where the job is over, say so and explain why rather than letting it surface in accounting.
  • Confirm every approved addition was captured through a revision or change order.
Closing with the client
  • Confirm the project is complete to the client's satisfaction.
  • Resolve any outstanding concern before the file closes.
  • Record the completion on the tracking spreadsheet.
Project Coordinator

For the coordinator taking the file to billing. Get it out clean and get it collected.

Done when — The invoice is submitted with complete documentation, and the receivable is being followed.
Billing readiness
  1. Confirm the Project Manager has released the file and confirmed budget.
  2. Verify documentation is complete — photos, readings, logs, authorizations, change orders, and permit records.
  3. Coordinate invoicing documentation with Accounting.
  4. Submit and record the submission date.
Clearing barriers
  • Where documentation is missing, name what is missing and who owns it rather than holding the file silently.
  • Escalate to the Project Manager when a file has been sitting.
  • The Division Manager reviews unbilled work — a file stuck here will be asked about.
Collections
  • Follow the receivable to paid.
  • Monitor aging and follow up on unpaid invoices.
  • Escalate to the Project Manager when a balance is stuck.
  • Close the loop with post-completion client follow-up.
← Back

Standard operating procedure · Company-Wide

Lead Intake & Estimating

Lead in, estimate out, file handed to the division that does the work.

Every job that starts with an estimate rather than an emergency dispatch begins here. This procedure describes the seven control points a lead passes through and what each role does at each one. At conversion, the file transfers to the division that will do the work.

Process owner: Sales Manager  ·  Compliance owner: Project Coordinator Manager

The process

1

Intake, Assignment & Scheduling

Every lead is captured, opened in DASH and CompanyCam, assigned, and scheduled with the customer.

Estimating Coordinator · Estimator — First Contact

2

Inspection

The property is inspected, every room the scope will reach is identified, and the customer is told when their estimate will arrive.

Estimator — Onsite · Estimator — Documentation

3

Writing the Estimate

The estimate is written claims-ready in Xactimate, reconciled where the work is complete, and delivered inside the turnaround standard.

Estimator

4

Review & Approval

Losses over $25,000 and anything off budget are reviewed by the Sales Manager before delivery.

Estimator · Sales Manager

5

Delivery & Follow-Up

The estimate reaches the customer or the adjuster, and is followed until there is an answer.

Estimator · Estimating Coordinator

6

Conversion & Handoff

Approval is secured, the file is prepped and transferred, and the receiving division captures the signature.

Estimator · Estimating Coordinator · Receiving Project Coordinator

7

Consulting Jobs (CST)

Consulting work is coordinated, invoiced, and collected here. It never transfers to a division.

Estimating Coordinator

This document says HOW the work runs. What each role owns lives in that role’s definition. Roles are named by title, never by person, so the procedure stays correct when someone changes seats.

Step by step

1

Intake, Assignment & Scheduling

Every lead is captured, opened in DASH and CompanyCam, assigned, and scheduled with the customer.
Estimating Coordinator

For the coordinator taking in a new lead: a direct call or email from the customer, or a referral in from someone at CELCO. Capture it completely and get an estimator on it the same day.

Done when — The lead is captured with every required field, the job is open in DASH and CompanyCam, an estimator is assigned, and the appointment is on the company calendar.
Capture at intake
  • Full name, phone, and email of the contact.
  • Property address.
  • Referral source.
  • Insurance carrier and claim details, where the job is a claim.
  • Financial responsibility: who is paying. Insurance, the customer as self-pay, an HOA, a property manager, or another party.
  • Brief description of the job.
Emergency screen — do this first
  1. Establish on the call whether the loss is active or the customer needs someone onsite now.
  2. If it requires immediate dispatch, send it straight to the Emergency Division so its Project Coordinator can prepare the division to dispatch. Do not hold it in the estimating queue.
  3. If the customer is requesting an inspection or estimate before any technician dispatch, continue through this procedure.
  4. Record which way it was routed and who received it.
Job setup
  • Open the job in DASH and CompanyCam as soon as the lead is captured — before an estimator is assigned.
  • Notate the intake information in DASH.
  • Chase whoever took the call for anything missing. An incomplete intake becomes a delayed estimate.
Assigning the estimator
  1. Assign based on current estimator workload and proximity to the property.
  2. Notify the assigned estimator so they can make contact and set the inspection.
  3. Place the estimator on the company calendar once they report back the date and time they agreed with the customer. The calendar follows the customer’s confirmation, not the assignment.
  4. Rebalance when a lead is sitting or an estimator is over capacity. Say so rather than letting the queue build.
Estimator — First Contact

For the estimator receiving a new assignment. Reach the customer, learn what the intake call could not capture, and set the inspection.

Done when — The customer has been contacted, the job detail is gathered, and the inspection is scheduled. The confirmed date and time are back with the Project Coordinator.
Making contact
  1. Contact the customer promptly once the lead is assigned to you.
  2. Introduce yourself and CELCO as the estimator who will handle their job.
  3. Confirm the property address and the onsite contact against the intake record.
  4. Correct the intake record where what you are told differs from what was captured.
Gathering detail
  • Ask what happened, when it was discovered, and what has been done since.
  • Establish whether the source is active, stopped, or repaired.
  • Establish occupancy, access, and any hazard before you arrive rather than after.
  • Confirm the insurance position: carrier, claim number, adjuster, or a clear non-insurance job.
Scheduling the inspection
  1. Agree a date and time with the customer directly.
  2. Report the confirmed appointment to the Project Coordinator so it goes on the company calendar.
  3. Keep the commitment once it is booked.
  4. Where an appointment has to move, tell the customer and the Project Coordinator before it, not after.
2

Inspection

The property is inspected, every room the scope will reach is identified, and the customer is told when their estimate will arrive.
Estimator — Onsite

For the estimator at the property. Inspect what is in front of you, and work out what else the scope will have to reach.

Done when — The loss is inspected, every affected room is identified along with any room the scope will consequentially reach, and the customer knows when their estimate will arrive.
Onsite
  1. Confirm access and meet the contact you scheduled with.
  2. Explain what you will be doing onsite before you start: what you will inspect, what you will document, and roughly how long it will take.
  3. Inspect the loss or the scope of work requested.
  4. Identify affected materials and areas, including adjacent, above, below, and concealed areas.
  5. Confirm what you find against what you were told on the scheduling call, and note any difference.
Rooms the scope will reach
  • Document every affected room.
  • Determine which additional rooms will consequentially become part of the scope, and document those the same way.
  • Hidden damage is the first cause: what sits behind, above, or below the visible loss.
  • Continuous materials are the second: flooring, paint, and trim that run from an affected room into an unaffected one cannot be stopped at the doorway.
  • A room found now is scope. The same room found later is a supplement.
Before you leave
  1. Recap what you found and what happens next.
  2. Ask the customer directly whether they have questions about the process or what was explained.
  3. Tell them when their estimate will be delivered, every time, on every inspection.
  4. Base that commitment on the turnaround standard in step 3, not on how your week looks.
  5. Where the loss is large or complex enough that the standard will not hold, say so onsite rather than missing it later.
Estimator — Documentation

For the estimator documenting the inspection. Capture it well enough that the estimate can be written from the record rather than from memory.

Done when — The sketch, photographs, and measurements are complete in Xactimate and CompanyCam, and the DASH job file is notated.
Sketch onsite
  • Sketch the property while you are onsite. Do not leave it for the office.
  • Include every door and window opening.
  • Include reference blocks: cabinets, showers, tubs, vanities, hearths, and anything similar.
  • Capture measurements as you sketch, so the sketch and the numbers agree.
Photographs
  1. Take wide-out views of every affected room, so the space reads as a whole.
  2. Take closeups of the damage itself.
  3. Take detail shots: open cabinets, and profiles of materials wherever a profile can be seen.
  4. Photograph the rooms the scope will consequentially reach, not only the obviously affected ones.
  5. Photograph proof of continuous scope: the material running unbroken from an affected room into the next one.
  6. Photograph anything an adjuster will question. Grade of material, installation type, and any complexity that justifies the price.
Required tools by job type
  • Matterport 3D on large or complex jobs.
  • Moisture meters and infrared on mitigation jobs.
Where it goes
  • Sketch and measurements built in Xactimate.
  • Photo documentation complete in CompanyCam.
  • DASH job file notated.
  • Any hazard, access limit, permit, or architectural committee review requirement recorded.
3

Writing the Estimate

The estimate is written claims-ready in Xactimate, reconciled where the work is complete, and delivered inside the turnaround standard.
Estimator

For the estimator writing the estimate. Xactimate claims-ready is the default. Completed emergency work carries an extra reconciliation before it leaves your hands.

Done when — The estimate is written, reconciled and budget-checked where the work is complete, and either ready to send or routed for review under step 4.
Format
  • Write the estimate yourself in Xactimate, claims-ready, as the standard for all work.
  • Every Xactimate estimate is written in CELCO format, with trade and activity headers separating the work in each room.
  • Proposal format may be used only where the job is a strict remodel or capital improvement with no possibility of becoming an insurance claim.
  • A proposal-format estimate still has to meet budget and margin requirements before it is sent. The format changes. The standard does not.
Turnaround from inspection
  1. Under $10,000 — estimate delivered within 24 hours.
  2. Over $10,000 — estimate delivered within 48 hours.
  3. Large losses over $100,000 — a preliminary estimate ready within 72 hours. Complexity varies widely on these, and they are the exception.
  4. In every case, the turnaround you committed to onsite is the one that applies.
Completed emergency work
  • Reconcile every emergency estimate against the mitigation equipment logs. The Emergency Project Coordinator places those logs in DASH.
  • Check the estimate against the budget spreadsheet to confirm it meets the budget standard set for that job. This check applies to completed emergency work.
  • An estimate that falls short of budget thresholds goes to the Sales Manager instead of the customer.
4

Review & Approval

Losses over $25,000 and anything off budget are reviewed by the Sales Manager before delivery.
Estimator

For the estimator deciding whether an estimate goes out or goes up for review. When any of these is true, it goes up.

Done when — The estimate triggers no review and is ready to deliver. Where review was required, every revision the Sales Manager noted has been made.
Route to the Sales Manager when
  • The loss is over $25,000.
  • The estimate falls short of the budget threshold for the job.
  • The scope carries complex trades: framing, kitchens, showers, roofs, or siding and stucco.
  • You are unsure whether the scope or the pricing will hold.
How to send it up
  • Send the estimate and the scope, and say why it is being reviewed.
  • Photos do not need to be attached. The Sales Manager reviews them in CompanyCam.
  • Where it is off budget, say by how much and why rather than leaving it to be found.
  • Do not deliver to the customer or the adjuster while a review is open.
  • Make every revision the Sales Manager notes before the estimate goes out.
Sales Manager

For the Sales Manager reviewing an estimate before it leaves CELCO. This is the last point at which scope and price can be corrected cheaply.

Done when — The estimate is approved to send, returned with required changes, or re-scoped — and the estimator knows which.
What you are reviewing for
  • Whether the scope reflects the work the job actually requires.
  • Whether pricing meets CELCO's budget and margin requirements.
  • Whether the estimate will hold up with the carrier or the adjuster.
  • Whether it reflects estimating best practices. This review is also how the standard gets taught.
Coaching in the field
  • The review teaches the estimate. Ride-alongs teach the inspection.
  • Join an occasional inspection as a quality check and a coaching opportunity. This is a periodic sample, not attendance at every inspection.
  • Spread ride-alongs across the team so every estimator is seen in the field from time to time.
  • Watch inspection quality, documentation discipline, and how the estimator handles the customer.
  • Coach onsite while the job is in front of you.
Returning the review
  1. Give the estimator a clear answer: send, change, or re-scope.
  2. Where you require changes, name them specifically.
  3. Return the review inside the job's turnaround window — a review that stalls becomes a missed commitment to the customer.
  4. Escalate to the C-suite where the exposure or the exception warrants it.
5

Delivery & Follow-Up

The estimate reaches the customer or the adjuster, and is followed until there is an answer.
Estimator

For the estimator after the estimate is written. Written is not delivered, and delivered is not answered.

Done when — The estimate is in the customer's or the adjuster's hands, the send is recorded in the job file, and follow-up is underway.
Deliver it as a package
  • Send the estimate with its supporting documentation as one package, not as an estimate on its own.
  • Mitigation and remediation: estimate, photo report, moisture and equipment logs, testing results, and clearance results.
  • Repairs: estimate, photo report, specialty subcontractor bids, ITEL reports, permits, and plans.
  • Include whatever else that particular job needs to stand on its own with an adjuster.
Sending
  1. Send the package to the customer, the adjuster, or both as the job requires.
  2. Record the delivery and the date in the DASH job file.
  3. Confirm receipt. An estimate written but not received has not been delivered.
Following up
  • Follow up with the adjuster or the customer until there is a decision.
  • Answer questions on scope and pricing directly.
  • Negotiate at your own discretion while the outcome stays budget positive, including minor reductions in scope.
  • Bring the Sales Manager in before agreeing anything that takes the job over budget or cuts significant scope.
  • Where a supplement or revision is required, write it to the same standard and the same review triggers.
Supplements: stay with the job
  • Stay in communication with the Project Manager for as long as the job runs.
  • The PM sees what the field uncovers. You are the one who can turn it into a supplement.
  • Ask what has changed rather than waiting to be told.
  • A supplement opportunity that leaks away is money CELCO earned and did not bill.
Estimating Coordinator

For the coordinator holding the estimating pipeline. Nothing sits silently.

Done when — Every inspected lead has an estimate that has been sent, and no lead is stalling without the Sales Manager knowing.
Following the queue
  • Follow up with estimators after every inspection to confirm the estimate is written and sent.
  • Confirm estimates reach the customer or the adjuster.
  • Assist with adjuster and customer follow-up where your workload permits. The estimator owns the follow-up, but a stalled estimate is everyone's problem.
  • Keep the Sales Manager visible on leads that are stalling.
6

Conversion & Handoff

Approval is secured, the file is prepped and transferred, and the receiving division captures the signature.
Estimator

For the estimator whose estimate has been approved. Approval reaches you first, so the file cannot move until you pass it on.

Done when — Approval from the carrier and the customer is in hand, the Project Coordinator has been told, and the scope and components sheets are with them for upload.
Securing approval
  1. Secure approval from the carrier and from the customer. Verbal or email is enough at this stage.
  2. Record who approved, when, and in what form.
  3. Tell the Estimating Coordinator as soon as you have it.
  4. Formal signature is captured later by the receiving division. Do not wait for it before reporting the approval.
Repair estimates
  • Send the Xactimate scope and components sheets to the Estimating Coordinator.
  • They upload both to DASH before the file is handed off.
  • Do this before the handoff, not after. The receiving division works from what is in DASH.
Estimating Coordinator

For the coordinator converting an approved estimate. Record the approval, prep the file, and hand it over clean enough to work the day it arrives.

Done when — The approval is recorded in DASH, the job file is prepped, and it has been reassigned to the receiving division's Project Coordinator, who has acknowledged it.
Approval
  • The estimator reports the approval. Confirm who approved, when, and in what form.
  • Verbal or email approval from the carrier and the customer is enough to move the file.
  • Record the approval in DASH before the handoff.
  • Formal signature is not captured here. The receiving division's Project Coordinator does that.
Where it goes
  1. Emergency work converted — prep the file and reassign it to the Emergency Project Coordinator, who sends the Work Authorization for signature through PandaDoc.
  2. Structure repairs converted — prep the file and reassign it to the Structure Project Coordinator, who sends the contract for signature through PandaDoc.
  3. Consulting work does not hand off. It stays here. See step 7.
  4. Confirm the receiving coordinator has acknowledged the assignment. Do not assume the notification was seen.
Prepped file standard
  • Complete intake record with financial responsibility and claim details.
  • Approved estimate and scope.
  • Approval recorded: who approved, when, and in what form.
  • For repairs, the Xactimate scope and components sheets uploaded to DASH.
  • Inspection photos in CompanyCam and the DASH job file current.
  • Any permit or architectural committee review the estimator flagged, noted for the division.
After the handoff
  • Once a file is reassigned it belongs to the receiving division. This role does not carry it forward.
  • Send anything that arrives afterward to the receiving coordinator rather than acting on it.
Receiving Project Coordinator

For the Emergency or Structure coordinator taking the file. You own it from this point — start by confirming what you were handed.

Done when — You have acknowledged the assignment, the signature document is out through PandaDoc, and DASH shows your division on the job.
On receipt
  1. Acknowledge the assignment so the estimating coordinator knows it landed.
  2. Check the file against the prepped-file standard and name anything missing the same day.
  3. Capture formal approval through PandaDoc — Work Authorization for emergency work, contract for scheduled work. The estimating side secured the approval. The signature is yours to collect.
  4. Update DASH so the Project Coordinator and Project Manager on the job are your division's. DASH does the tracking.
What transfers with the file
  • Ownership of the job file, the client relationship, and everything downstream.
  • The approved scope — work to it, and raise a gap with the estimator rather than discovering it onsite.
  • The permit or architectural committee review flag, if the estimator raised one. Start that process on receipt, not at schedule.
7

Consulting Jobs (CST)

Consulting work is coordinated, invoiced, and collected here. It never transfers to a division.
Estimating Coordinator

For the coordinator carrying CELCO's consulting book. These jobs are the exception to everything in step 6. They run start to finish here.

Done when — The consulting job is complete, invoiced to the hiring party, and the balance is collected or actively being pursued.
Running the job
  • Coordinate consulting jobs end to end. These stay with this role and are never handed to a division.
  • Keep consulting job files documented to the same standard as any other job.
  • Track the consulting book separately so it stays visible. No division is watching it.
Invoicing and collections
  1. Request invoicing to the hiring party once the consulting work is complete.
  2. Record the invoice and the submission date.
  3. Follow the receivable to paid — outreach and follow-up on consulting invoices are yours.
  4. Escalate a stuck balance to the Sales Manager rather than letting it age quietly.

Standard operating procedure · Emergency Division

Emergency Response

The call, the first response, and the decision that follows it.

An emergency call is the one moment CELCO cannot redo. This procedure covers the four control points between the phone ringing and the job entering daily monitoring. Speed matters here, but a fast response that leaves no record costs more than it saves.

Process owner: Division Manager  ·  Compliance owner: Project Coordinator Manager

The process

1

The Call

The intake is complete, a responder has accepted, and the caller knows what happens next.

Project Coordinator

2

First Response

The property is stabilized and the loss is documented well enough that nobody has to guess later.

Lead Technician — Onsite · Lead Technician — Documentation

3

The Decision

The Project Manager sets the scope and the next action, and the file is complete enough to act on.

Project Manager · Project Coordinator

4

Management Exception

Serious losses get the resources, decisions, and escalation they need, without the DM taking over the PM's job.

Division Manager

This document says HOW the work runs. What each role owns lives in that role’s definition. Roles are named by title, never by person, so the procedure stays correct when someone changes seats.

Step by step

1

The Call

The intake is complete, a responder has accepted, and the caller knows what happens next.
Project Coordinator

For whoever answers the emergency line. Gather the facts, dispatch a responder, and leave the caller informed.

Done when — The intake is captured in full, a named responder has accepted with an ETA, and the caller has been told who is coming and when.
Safety first
  1. Ask whether anyone is in immediate danger. Direct life-safety emergencies to 911 and keep people out of unsafe areas.
  2. Establish whether the source is active, stopped, or repaired, and who stopped it.
  3. Record any water, ceiling, odor, contamination, electrical, or structural hazard.
  4. Note whether management, engineering, security, a plumber, the fire department, or 911 has already been contacted.
Capture at intake
  • Caller name, callback number, email, and their title or company.
  • Property, unit or area, full address, and the onsite contact with a phone number.
  • Access, parking, security, and gate instructions.
  • Who authorized the work, and the billing party.
  • Work order, PO, or claim number where one exists.
  • Emergency type, what happened, and when it was discovered.
Dispatch
  1. Post the intake to Slack: caller, property, affected area, incident, source status, hazards, access, authorization, and billing or claim detail.
  2. Call the primary on-call technician. Slack alone is not a dispatch.
  3. Obtain acceptance, a departure estimate, an arrival estimate, and any staffing or equipment need.
  4. If there is no answer, call again and text after five minutes. Then call the backup responder and escalate to the after-hours manager.
  5. Update Slack with the assigned responder, the ETA, and the caller-contact status.
Before you end the call
  • Repeat the address, unit, callback number, and emergency type back to the caller.
  • Tell them who is coming, roughly when, and what happens next.
  • Promise no coverage, no final pricing, and no arrival time before the responder has confirmed it.
2

First Response

The property is stabilized and the loss is documented well enough that nobody has to guess later.
Lead Technician — Onsite

For the first responder at the property. Make it safe, find the whole loss, and stabilize what you are authorized to stabilize.

Done when — The property is safe, the source and every affected area are identified, and the authorized stabilization is complete.
Arrival
  1. Confirm the correct property and unit, meet the onsite contact, and identify who has authority to approve work.
  2. Perform an immediate safety assessment. Stop and escalate electrical, structural, gas, sewage, contamination, or suspected regulated-material hazards.
  3. Identify the reported source, its current status, and who stopped or repaired it.
  4. Inspect the areas the loss reaches: adjacent, opposite-side, above, below, cabinet, flooring, and crawlspace.
Authorization
  • Obtain the required authorization before performing work, and document it.
  • Where approval is verbal, record who gave it and when.
  • Record refusals, access limits, and anything left pending.
  • Work beyond what was authorized needs the Project Manager first.
Stabilize
  1. Determine category and drying class from what you observed, not from what you expect.
  2. Perform the authorized extraction, demolition, cleaning, and containment.
  3. Place equipment and record it by room and identification number.
  4. Leave the jobsite clean and properly set up.
Lead Technician — Documentation

For the same responder, before you leave. The initial packet is the whole record of a moment nobody can revisit.

Done when — Photographs, readings, a sketch, and the initial note are uploaded onsite, and the Project Manager has been called.
Photographs
  • Take wide and close photographs BEFORE disturbing materials.
  • Cover the address, the source, every affected area, pre-existing conditions, and meter displays.
  • Photograph equipment placement once it is set.
Readings and sketch
  • Record readings by room, by material, and by exact location.
  • Establish a dry standard or an unaffected comparison, and record psychrometric conditions.
  • Sketch the property showing the source, affected areas, demolition, and equipment placement.
The initial note must state
  • Who provided access, who was onsite, who authorized the response, and who was contacted.
  • The reported source, whether CELCO confirmed it, and the source status.
  • Every affected area and material observed, including concealed or inaccessible areas.
  • Safety conditions, readings, dry standard, and the category and class reasoning.
  • Work performed with quantities, and equipment installed by room and ID.
  • Approvals, refusals, customer concerns, and the next action.
Before departure
  1. Call the Project Manager with findings, work completed, recommended scope, blockers, and next visit.
  2. Upload the complete packet onsite. Paperwork written later from memory is not acceptable.
  3. Report facts and outcomes. The technical decision is the Project Manager’s to make and document.
3

The Decision

The Project Manager sets the scope and the next action, and the file is complete enough to act on.
Project Manager

For the PM turning a first response into a decision. Reviewing the packet does not move the job forward. Directing the work does.

Done when — The stabilization scope is decided, the next visit has a purpose and a date, and the decision is documented in the job file.
Review with the responder
  1. Speak with the technician before they leave the property.
  2. Review source and source status, affected areas, safety conditions, readings, photographs, category and class, equipment, and work performed.
  3. Decide whether the investigation is complete, or whether more rooms, cavities, flooring, crawlspace, plumbing, or building systems must be inspected.
Direct the work
  • Set the authorized stabilization scope: extraction, demolition, cleaning, containment, air filtration, drying, specialty drying, contents movement, or temporary protection.
  • Confirm whether further approval, testing, plumber work, environmental review, building access, or relocation is required.
  • Tell the technician what must be finished before leaving and what stays pending.
  • Tell the Project Coordinator what to schedule, obtain, communicate, and follow up.
Document the decision
  • Current condition: source status, affected areas, hazards, and drying or demolition status.
  • Decision: stabilize, expand inspection, demo, test, hold, obtain approval, relocate, or refer to another trade.
  • Reason, tied to readings, photographs, site conditions, category and class, or authorization.
  • Action plan: who does what, by when, and what the next visit must accomplish.
  • The responsible party, the deadline, and the next review date.
Escalate to the Division Manager
  • High-risk, large, multi-unit, contaminated, customer-sensitive, or resource-intensive losses go up.
  • So does any job you cannot complete safely or within your authority.
Project Coordinator

For the coordinator building the file. Review the packet while the technician can still fix it today.

Done when — The job record is complete, the initial packet has been accepted rather than merely received, and the next visit is scheduled.
Set the file up
  1. Confirm the dispatch was accepted, and that the caller, onsite contact, address, unit, access instructions, source information, and ETA are correct.
  2. Create or update the job record with customer, property, billing, claim, adjuster, management-company, and referral information.
  3. Send the technician the complete intake, photographs, access instructions, building restrictions, work-order requirements, and account-specific procedures.
  4. Confirm the required authorizations and notices are available, and identify who can sign onsite.
The same-day review
  • Review the initial packet while corrections can still be made the same day. This timing is the point of the review.
  • Return missing items with the EXACT correction required: the form, reading, equipment entry, photograph, signature, or note detail.
  • Flag any authority or billing uncertainty to the Project Manager immediately.
  • Review for completeness and consistency. The technical decision belongs to the Project Manager.
Ready for daily monitoring
  • Job and contact information complete enough to schedule and communicate.
  • Responder, arrival status, and onsite contact documented.
  • Authorization, billing, claim, and work-order requirements identified.
  • Paperwork, readings, photographs, equipment information, and the technician note uploaded.
  • No blank required fields and no unexplained conflicts.
  • The PM decision, current status, next action, and deadline documented.
  • The next visit scheduled and assigned.
4

Management Exception

Serious losses get the resources, decisions, and escalation they need, without the DM taking over the PM's job.
Division Manager

For the DM on an escalated loss. Manage through the Project Manager. Do not replace their technical role.

Done when — The PM has a defensible stabilization plan, the resources to execute it, and a documented escalation path.
When to step in
  • Category 3, sewage, contamination, suspected regulated materials, or environmental testing.
  • Multiple units, common areas, commercial operations, high-rise access, or significant business interruption.
  • Active or unidentified source, structural concern, electrical exposure, ceiling collapse, or unsafe occupancy.
  • Large equipment or labor demand, specialty drying, crawlspace work, contents pack-out, or relocation.
  • Customer, account, adjuster, ownership, authorization, or coverage sensitivity.
  • The PM decision or the next action is missing.
  • The response exceeds what can be done safely, or exceeds available authority.
What to require
  1. Make the PM state the source status, affected areas, safety risks, current scope, authorization status, resource needs, and next action.
  2. Confirm the response has the staffing, equipment, PPE, containment, vendors, plumber support, environmental resources, and building access it needs.
  3. Resolve or assign after-hours staffing, equipment shortages, customer relocation, contents, access, work-order limits, and account-specific requirements.
  4. Approve management-level exceptions: emergency vendor use, unusual costs, or delayed work where company policy requires it.
Questions you must be able to answer
  • What is the immediate risk, and has the property been stabilized?
  • What remains unknown, and who is resolving it?
  • Does the PM have the authority, staffing, equipment, and outside resources they need?
  • What must happen next, by when, and what escalation is required?
Close the exception
  • Set deadlines for unresolved source, access, testing, authorization, or staffing issues, and follow up through the PM.
  • Decide whether executive, client, property-management, broker, or account communication is required.
  • Confirm the job moves into daily monitoring with a named PM, a clear objective, a planned visit, and a documented escalation path.
← Back

Standard operating procedure · Emergency Division

Daily Monitoring

Every drying day, from the visit to the decision.

A job in monitoring is a job costing money every day it sits. This procedure runs once per visit, for as many days as the job is drying. Each visit has to produce a daily monitoring packet the coordinator can process and a decision the Project Manager can act on, the same day.

Process owner: Division Manager  ·  Compliance owner: Project Coordinator Manager

The process

1

The Visit

Every active area is checked, every reading is taken, and the daily monitoring packet is uploaded before the technician leaves.

Water Damage Technician

2

The Same-Day Review

Incomplete paperwork is corrected the same day, while the technician is still able to fix it.

Project Coordinator

3

The Daily Decision

Every visit becomes a same-day decision with an assigned action and a documented reason.

Project Manager

4

Active-Job Oversight

No active job sits without a current status, a next action, and a responsible owner.

Division Manager

This document says HOW the work runs. What each role owns lives in that role’s definition. Roles are named by title, never by person, so the procedure stays correct when someone changes seats.

Step by step

1

The Visit

Every active area is checked, every reading is taken, and the daily monitoring packet is uploaded before the technician leaves.
Water Damage Technician

For the technician onsite. Do the work, record it where it happened, and report a clear outcome before you leave.

Done when — Every active area is inspected, readings and equipment are recorded, the daily note is written, and the daily monitoring packet is uploaded onsite.
Onsite
  1. Confirm the correct job, date, technician, hours, visit type, category, and class.
  2. Inspect every active affected area and confirm the source has not recurred.
  3. Count every piece of equipment by type and room. Record additions, removals, moves, shutdowns, and operating problems.
  4. Record moisture readings for every active material and area, using consistent monitoring points and the correct meter scale.
  5. Enter the dry standard or unaffected comparison, and complete the psychrometric and dehumidifier fields.
Photographs
  • Wide-angle shots showing the room as a whole.
  • Equipment in place.
  • Work in progress.
  • Representative meter readings.
The daily note must state
  • Who provided access, who was onsite, and who was contacted.
  • Conditions on arrival, including equipment status, source status, hazards, and changes since the prior visit.
  • Moisture and environmental results: what improved, stalled, got wetter, or reached the dry goal.
  • Exact work performed by room, material, and quantity.
  • Equipment added, removed, repositioned, shut down, or left onsite, and why.
  • Approvals, refusals, access limits, customer concerns, testing, or other blockers.
  • Current job status, exact next action, responsible person, and planned visit date.
The field standard
  • Write the note at the property and upload the daily monitoring packet before leaving.
  • “Demo”, “monitor”, and “checked equipment” describe nothing. Say what, where, and how much.
  • Blank required fields, unsupported takedown, and unexplained equipment changes are not acceptable.
  • Report facts and outcomes. The technical decision is the Project Manager’s.
2

The Same-Day Review

Incomplete paperwork is corrected the same day, while the technician is still able to fix it.
Project Coordinator

For the coordinator reviewing today's daily monitoring packets. You are the completeness gate, not the technical reviewer.

Done when — Every scheduled visit has a daily monitoring packet, corrections have been returned and received, and the Project Manager knows about every exception.
Check it arrived
  1. Confirm a daily monitoring packet was received for every scheduled visit.
  2. Verify the correct job, date, technician, and visit type.
  3. Review the paperwork while the technician can still correct it today.
Check it is consistent
  • Compare equipment counts with the prior visit, the photographs, and the documented additions or removals.
  • Confirm readings cover every active room and material, and include the dry standard or unaffected comparison.
  • Confirm the psychrometric and dehumidifier sections are complete, or carry a specific reason they could not be.
  • Confirm the photographs support the work, readings, equipment placement, and condition described in the note.
The completeness gate
  • Header, date, hours, visit type, category, and class are complete.
  • Every required field is completed, marked not applicable, or explained.
  • Equipment is listed by room and changes are explained.
  • Moisture, dry standard, and environmental readings are complete.
  • Photographs are uploaded, dated, and consistent with the note.
  • The note identifies the visit outcome and the next action.
  • Customer, adjuster, or property communication is documented where it applies.
  • The next visit, vendor action, approval, or follow-up is scheduled from PM direction.
Returning work
  • Return incomplete or contradictory paperwork with the exact correction required.
  • Accept the daily monitoring packet only after the corrections come back.
  • Notify the Project Manager promptly of technical questions, approvals, delays, access issues, or a job with no defined next step.
3

The Daily Decision

Every visit becomes a same-day decision with an assigned action and a documented reason.
Project Manager

For the PM each day a job is drying. Reviewing the file does not move the job. Making and communicating a decision does.

Done when — Today's decision is made, documented with its reason, and communicated to both the technician and the coordinator.
Review
  1. Read the technician’s note, moisture trend, psychrometrics, equipment, photographs, work performed, and current scope.
  2. Speak with the technician the same day to clarify findings and confirm what occurred onsite.
  3. Confirm the change since the prior visit is measurable and supported.
Decide
  • Continue drying, change equipment, perform additional demolition, await testing or approval, proceed to takedown, or move to repair handoff.
  • Confirm the next visit has a defined purpose and is scheduled at the correct interval.
  • Address access, authorization, environmental, contents, customer, adjuster, vendor, staffing, and equipment blockers.
Document and direct
  • Status: what is dry, what remains affected, and whether progress is acceptable.
  • Decision, with the reason tied to readings, photographs, conditions, or authorization.
  • Action: who does what, by when, and what the next visit must accomplish.
  • The responsible person, the deadline, and the next review date.
  • The technician knows the next onsite objective.
  • The coordinator knows what to schedule, obtain, communicate, and follow up.
Escalate
  • Unresolved blockers, stalled drying, scope conflicts, high equipment days, or repeated documentation failures go to the Division Manager.
4

Active-Job Oversight

No active job sits without a current status, a next action, and a responsible owner.
Division Manager

For the DM working the division’s active jobs. Manage through the Project Managers rather than waiting for technicians or coordinators to unstick jobs.

Done when — Every exception has an owner, a deadline, and a follow-up date, and stalled jobs have a management plan.
Work the exceptions
  1. Review overdue paperwork, missed visits, stalled drying, pending approvals, and jobs without a defined next action.
  2. Require each PM to state the current condition, decision, next action, responsible person, and deadline for every exception.
  3. Challenge jobs that remain in monitoring without measurable progress or a clear reason for continued equipment days.
  4. Resolve or assign action for staffing, equipment, access, environmental, vendor, customer, adjuster, authorization, and claim blockers.
What good looks like
  • Every active job has a current status, next action, and responsible owner.
  • Every blocker has a deadline and an escalation path.
  • PM decisions are supported by readings, photographs, notes, and approvals.
  • Monitoring frequency and equipment days are justified.
  • Missed or incomplete paperwork is being corrected rather than ignored.
  • Stalled jobs have a management plan and a follow-up date.
  • Takedown jobs are moving to billing and repair handoff.
Questions to ask the PM
  • What changed since the last visit, and what evidence supports it?
  • What decision did you make, and did the technician and coordinator receive clear direction?
  • What is preventing the next step, who owns it, and when will it be resolved?
  • Why is equipment still onsite, or what supports takedown and closure?
Patterns, not just jobs
  • Confirm PMs are speaking with technicians and documenting decisions rather than merely reviewing forms.
  • Identify repeated documentation, scheduling, or decision failures and assign coaching or corrective action.
  • Confirm completed mitigation jobs move promptly to equipment reconciliation, billing review, and repair handoff.

Standard operating procedure · Emergency Division

Billing & Claim Resolution

From equipment pickup to money in the door.

The work is finished and the money is not. This procedure covers the four control points between equipment pickup and payment. A file that sits here has already cost CELCO the labor, the equipment, and the risk, and is earning nothing back. On claim work the invoice follows carrier agreement, because an invoice issued before agreement puts a number in receivables that nobody has agreed to pay.

Process owner: Division Manager  ·  Compliance owner: Project Coordinator Manager

The process

1

Billing Turnover

The field file is closed when the equipment comes out and no further mitigation work is scheduled.

Lead Technician

2

Scope Confirmation & Estimator Request

The completed field file becomes a defensible scope, and a named estimator is assigned to write it.

Project Manager · Project Coordinator

3

The Estimate & Carrier Agreement

The estimate is written from the record, submitted to the adjuster, and worked until CELCO and the carrier agree.

Estimator · Project Coordinator

4

Aging Oversight

No completed job goes more than five business days without meaningful activity.

Division Manager

This document says HOW the work runs. What each role owns lives in that role’s definition. Roles are named by title, never by person, so the procedure stays correct when someone changes seats.

Step by step

1

Billing Turnover

The field file is closed when the equipment comes out and no further mitigation work is scheduled.
Lead Technician

For the lead at equipment pickup, where the job has reached the dry standard and no further mitigation work is scheduled. The job is complete when the file is, not when the equipment is loaded.

Done when — Final readings, reconciled equipment, final photographs, and the work completed note are uploaded, and the PC and PM have been told mitigation is complete.
Close the field file
  1. Pull equipment only where the affected materials have reached the dry standard and no further mitigation work is scheduled.
  2. Take final moisture readings at every remaining monitoring point and identify the dry standard used.
  3. Reconcile all equipment by type, quantity, room, and equipment ID. Report missing or damaged units immediately.
  4. Take final wide-angle, close-up, meter-reading, equipment-removal, and remaining-repair photographs.
  5. Write the work completed note before leaving: what dried, what was removed, what remains open, and what still needs repair.
  6. Confirm the source status and document who reported or verified the repair.
  7. Upload final paperwork, readings, photographs, labor, materials, and equipment records before the end of the shift.
The work completed note must state
  • Equipment removal date and departure time.
  • Rooms and materials confirmed dry, including final readings.
  • Equipment removed, and any equipment remaining onsite.
  • Materials removed, cavities left open, and reconstruction needs.
  • Customer or property representative updated, and any concern raised.
  • Source repaired, stopped, active, or not independently verified.
  • Any missing approval, signature, access, photograph, reading, or unresolved item.
  • A clear statement that field documentation is complete, or a specific list of what remains.
What does not close a job
  • “Equipment picked up” or “job dry” without final readings and file status.
  • Blank notes, missing photographs, or unreconciled equipment.
  • An assumption that the PC, PM, or estimator will reconstruct the scope later from photographs.
  • Respond to correction requests the same day. A billing file waiting on field documentation is a job aging for no reason.
2

Scope Confirmation & Estimator Request

The completed field file becomes a defensible scope, and a named estimator is assigned to write it.
Project Manager

For the PM converting a finished job into a scope. You own the technical record the estimate gets built from.

Done when — The field record is confirmed complete and defensible, and every gap has a named owner and a same-day correction deadline.
Confirm the record
  1. Review the lead’s work completed note, final readings, photographs, equipment record, labor, materials, and authorizations within one business day.
  2. Speak with the lead where scope, quantities, drying result, special procedures, or unresolved conditions are unclear.
  3. Confirm the field record supports category, class, affected materials, demolition quantities, equipment days, labor, PPE, containment, cleaning, and disposal.
What the estimator will read
  • The estimator writes from the DASH notes, CompanyCam, and the daily monitoring packets. Those three are the scope record.
  • Where the record is thin, fix the record. Verbal scope direction disappears and leaves the estimate unsupported.
  • Answer estimator questions the same day, including a site visit where the file cannot settle it.
Support the estimator, do not take the file
  • The estimator owns the estimate, the adjuster conversation, and the negotiation strategy.
  • Support the estimator on technical responses, disputed line items, and supplements when asked.
  • Where the estimator raises a red flag on the scope or the documentation, respond the same day with a decision.
Project Coordinator

For the coordinator getting an estimator onto the file. You request the assignment. The Estimating Coordinator makes it.

Done when — The Estimating Coordinator has a complete request, an estimator is assigned with a due date, and both are recorded in DASH.
Take the file
  1. Review the completed job file by the end of the next business day after equipment removal.
  2. Confirm authorizations, customer and claim information, daily paperwork, notes, readings, equipment records, photographs, labor, materials, and the work completed note are present.
  3. Return incomplete work with the exact missing item, responsible person, and same-day correction deadline. Track it to completion.
Request the estimator
  1. Send the request to the Estimating Coordinator once the file is complete and the PM has confirmed the record.
  2. State the job, the equipment removal date, the claim position, and any condition the estimator has to know about.
  3. The Estimating Coordinator assigns the estimator and sets the due date. That assignment is hers to make.
  4. Confirm back who was assigned and what date the estimate is due, and record both in DASH.
The standard for a request
  • Send the file complete. An estimator chasing missing paperwork is an estimate arriving late.
  • Say what the file needs. “Please write this one up” is not a request.
  • Chase the assignment where it has not come back by the end of the next business day.
3

The Estimate & Carrier Agreement

The estimate is written from the record, submitted to the adjuster, and worked until CELCO and the carrier agree.
Estimator

For the estimator assigned an emergency file. You write it, you submit it, and you carry the adjuster conversation through to agreement.

Done when — The estimate is submitted to the adjuster, the follow-up cadence is running, and the coordinator is told the day agreement is reached.
Write it from the record
  1. Read the DASH notes, the CompanyCam photographs, and the daily monitoring packets before writing a line.
  2. Ask the PM for anything the record leaves unsettled, including a site visit where one is needed.
  3. Tie every billed activity to a note, photograph, reading, equipment record, labor record, or authorization.
  4. Tell the PM about a scope or documentation red flag before the estimate goes to the carrier.
Submit to the adjuster
  1. Send the estimate and the supporting package to the adjuster, copying the Project Coordinator.
  2. Record recipients, attachments, submission date, confirmation, and the assigned carrier reviewer.
  3. Handle the adjuster’s questions and feedback directly. The coordinator is copied so she can see where the file stands.
  4. Own the technical responses, the disputed line items, the supplements, and the negotiation strategy. Pull the PM in for support.
Carrier follow-up cadence
  1. Within 2 business days: confirm receipt, the assigned reviewer, missing items, and the expected review date.
  2. By 5 business days: call and email. Identify review status, coverage or causation issues, inspection needs, third-party review, disputed items, the undisputed amount, and a response date.
  3. By 10 business days: request the supervisor or claim-team contact, update the PC, escalate to the PM and DM, and establish a written response deadline.
  4. Every 5 business days thereafter: obtain a response, requested document, disputed item, deadline, payment commitment, escalation contact, or documented refusal to respond.
Follow-up that means something
  • Never send only “Any update?”. Ask what is preventing completion, who owns the step, what is needed, and the date it will be completed.
  • Ask whether an undisputed amount has been identified, and when CELCO should expect the written decision.
  • Document the answer, the responsible outside party, the next action, and the promised date in DASH.
  • Every file carries a current status, a named owner, an exact next action, and a next follow-up date.
Reaching agreement
  • Every disputed line item is resolved, withdrawn, or documented as the carrier’s refusal.
  • The agreed scope and the agreed amount are in writing from the carrier.
  • Supplements are submitted and agreed rather than left for the invoice to absorb.
  • The Project Coordinator is notified to request the invoice the same day agreement is reached.
Project Coordinator

For the coordinator supporting the file to paid. The estimator carries the carrier. You watch the calendar, close the gaps, and request the invoice when agreement lands.

Done when — Gap days are flagged to the estimator, the customer is current, and the invoice request goes to Accounting the same day the estimator reports agreement.
Watch the gap days
  • Track submission date, last carrier contact, next follow-up date, and the named hold-up for every emergency file in billing.
  • Flag the estimator where the cadence has a gap day. Support the follow-up rather than duplicating it.
  • Escalate to the PM and the Division Manager where a file goes 10 business days without a substantive carrier response.
Invoice on agreement
  1. Request the invoice from Accounting when the estimator reports written agreement with the carrier.
  2. Give Accounting the agreed scope and the agreed amount.
  3. Accounting issues the invoice through QuickBooks.
  4. Confirm the invoice went out, record it in DASH, and set the payment follow-up date.
Why the invoice waits
  • An invoice issued before agreement becomes a receivable the carrier has never agreed to pay.
  • That file reads as collectable on the Aging AR list while the real work left is a scope negotiation.
  • Where a partial or undisputed amount is agreed in writing, request that invoice and keep working the balance.
Keep the customer current
  • Update the customer at submission, when the carrier requests information, and when their balance changes.
  • Tell the customer where the file stands when the carrier is slow or disputes the estimate.
  • Answer the deductible and out-of-pocket question early. A surprise at invoicing becomes a collections problem.
4

Aging Oversight

No completed job goes more than five business days without meaningful activity.
Division Manager

For the DM working the Aging AR list. Manage billing exceptions through the PM, the estimator, and the PC, before a completed file becomes a collection emergency.

Done when — Every aged or disputed file has a stated obstacle, a responsible person, a deadline, and a management strategy.
The normal timeline
  1. Same-day field completion at equipment pickup.
  2. One business day for the PC and PM reviews.
  3. Estimator assigned by the Estimating Coordinator within one business day of the request.
  4. Two business days for the estimate.
  5. Same-day submission to the adjuster.
  6. Invoice requested the same day the carrier agrees, and issued by Accounting through QuickBooks.
The aging standard
  • 0 to 3 business days after pickup: file complete, PM-reviewed, estimator assigned.
  • 3 to 5 business days: estimate written and submitted to the adjuster.
  • 5 business days after submission: substantive carrier status and a named hold-up documented.
  • 10 business days after submission: PM and DM escalation, customer update, supervisor request, written response deadline.
  • Agreement reached: invoice requested the same business day and issued by Accounting.
  • Every completed job shows meaningful activity within five business days.
  • Every estimate has an assigned estimator and a due date.
Challenge the vague
  • “With estimating”, “under review”, “waiting on insurance”, and “no update” are not statuses.
  • Require the precise obstacle and the responsible person.
  • A file waiting on carrier agreement is a negotiation to work, rather than a file to park.
  • Ask what the carrier has already agreed to, and whether an undisputed amount can be invoiced now.
Questions you must be able to answer
  • What exactly is preventing this job from being estimated, agreed, invoiced, or paid?
  • Who owns the next action internally and externally, and what is the deadline?
  • What did the carrier request or dispute, and what amount is undisputed or at risk?
  • What management decision or escalation is required today?
